newsitem.title: UK: Dlr energy flags in quiet Europe, US data awaited.
newsitem.headline: Dlr energy flags in quiet Europe, US data awaited.

text.p: The dollar's energy waned by Europe's midsession as most European centres were closed for a holiday and what operators there were in the market sat back to wait for U.S. data due later in the day.

During the Asian session earlier, the dollar had risen to a fresh 55-month high against the yen while it had also rallied on the mark, supported by surprisingly strong U.S. economic data released on Wednesday.
"But there's some profit-taking in dollar/mark going on now, and there aren't many people going against it, with the market so thin," said a trader at a U.S. bank here.

The Australian dollar, for example, rose to a high of 100.05 yen overnight, its highest since May 1992. Ten-year Australian government bonds currently yield 7.930 percent compared with 2.325 percent for their Japanese counterparts.

Amid a lack of incentive in the European morning session, traders were awaiting the U.S. April National Association of Purchasing Managers (NAPM) data due at 1400 GMT, which was forecast to dip to 53.6 from March's 55.0.
The market was watching U.S. data even more keenly than usual following Wednesday's GDP, which showed the economy grew a blistering 5.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997.
U.S. March personal spending and income data are due at 1230 GMT, and are forecast to rise 0.4 and 0.5 percent respectively after increasing 0.9 and 0.3 percent the previous month.

Despite the dollar's bullish tone, some doubted whether strong figures today would be able to push the currency much higher, adding that market interest rates already appear to have priced in a rise in key U.S. rates.

"We got figures pointing to a robust economy yesterday so short-term (U.S.) interest rates should have risen, but they didn't react at all," said Isao Kaneko, senior dealer at DKB's international treasury division in London.

"It looks like it's going to be difficult for U.S. market rates to surge now as yesterday's moves mean there were a lot of positions in there which had priced in a rate hike. And since the dollar's been bought on expectations of higher rates, it's going to be hard to drive the dollar up for now," Kaneko said.
Moves in Eurodollar interest rate futures today show the market has factored in a U.S. rate hike to above six percent by September, with the September futures trading at 93.875.
The currency market will also be closely watching remarks by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, who is due to speak at a Chicago Fed conference on the banking industry at 1325 GMT.
The dollar was at 1.7268/73 marks at 1055 GMT, slipping from a high of 1.7334 seen in early European trade but still above 1.7213/18 in late Europe on Wednesday.

Against the yen, the dollar was at 127.05/15 after hitting 127.47 earlier according to Bank of Japan data, its highest level since August 1992. Dollar/yen was at 126.93/98 in late Europe on Wednesday.

Traders cited yen weakness against other currencies as well, with some saying the underlying trend of Japanese investors' money going overseas in search of higher yields had resurfaced in recent days.
The British pound, meanwhile, slipped against the mark and was steady against the dollar as the market awaited the results of today's parliamentary elections.
Opinion polls have consistently shown throughout Britain's six-week election campaign that the opposition Labour party was well ahead of the ruling Conservatives, who have been in power for 18 years.
